title: Consent to treatment: s58, s58A, s62 and s63
blurb: Apply the three-month medication rule, the ECT safeguards and urgent treatment powers before giving treatment.
question: Daniel has been detained under section 3 for 14 weeks and has received antipsychotic medication since his first day. He now refuses his evening dose. As his nurse, what must you check before giving the medication without his consent?

teach.body: Part 4 of the Act controls treatment for mental disorder given to detained patients. Some treatment can be given without consent (s63), but medication after three months (s58) and ECT (s58A) need extra safeguards, usually a certificate from a second opinion appointed doctor (SOAD). In plain English: detention allows treatment without consent, but the longer or more intrusive the treatment, the more independent checks the law demands.

head: Section
Treatment
Safeguard
rows: AC in charge directs; consent not needed
Capable consent certified, or SOAD certificate
Capable adult consent, or SOAD if incapable
Overrides s57 and s58 in tight cases

items.label: First medicine for mental disorder in this detention
s63: can be given without consent

teach.caption: The clock starts at the first medication in the current period of detention, not the date of detention.

children.label: SOAD certificate
children.sub: No conflict with advance decision, attorney, deputy, court

steps.label: SOAD visits
steps.sub: Not the RC or the AC in charge

steps.sub: Neither a nurse nor a doctor

teach.caption: s58(4), s58A(6); COP15 25.75. The two consultees cannot be the RC or the AC in charge.

rows.label: Alleviate serious suffering (not irreversible or hazardous)

teach.caption: Treatment must be immediately necessary. s62 is not a routine way round a missing certificate.

teach.body: Daniel's first dose was 14 weeks ago, so the three months have passed and s58 applies. Before giving medication without consent, you check the certificate kept with his chart (COP15 25.74-25.75): is there a SOAD certificate covering this drug, route and dose range, and does it reflect that he is refusing? A consent certificate is not enough once he refuses. If none applies, you do not give it and escalate to the AC; s62 is only for genuinely immediate necessity.

teach.text: The MCA cannot be used to authorise treatment for mental disorder that is regulated by Part 4 of the MHA (MCA s28). And a consent certificate (capable patient agrees) stops covering treatment the moment a capable patient withdraws consent: a SOAD certificate is then needed.

items: s63: most treatment for mental disorder can be given to detained patients without consent.
s58: after 3 months from the first medicine in this detention, consent must be certified or a SOAD must certify.
s58A: ECT cannot be given to a capable adult who refuses (s62 life-saving or serious deterioration aside); under-18s always need a SOAD.
SOAD consults a nurse and one person who is neither nurse nor doctor; nurses check the certificate before giving.

summary: You can now decide whether s63, s58, s58A or s62 governs a treatment, check a certificate before giving medication, and explain the extra protections for ECT. You can also explain why the MCA cannot be used for Part 4 treatment.

A.q: From when is the three-month period under section 58 measured?
options: The date the patient was first admitted to hospital
The first medicine given in this detention
The date of the latest renewal of detention
The first tribunal hearing
A.why: Section 58(1)(b): three months from the first occasion in the current period of detention when medicine was given for the mental disorder.

whyNot.0: The clock runs from the first medication in this detention, not admission.
whyNot.2: Renewal does not restart the three-month clock.
whyNot.3: Tribunal hearings have no effect on the s58 period.

A.q: A SOAD is preparing to certify medication for a patient who refuses. Whom must the SOAD consult?
options: The RC and the nearest relative
Two doctors professionally involved in the patient's care
A nurse and someone who is neither nurse nor doctor
The AMHP and the hospital managers
A.why: Section 58(4): two people professionally concerned with treatment, one a nurse and the other neither a nurse nor a doctor, and neither the RC nor the AC in charge.

whyNot.0: The RC is excluded as a consultee, and the nearest relative is not a statutory consultee.
whyNot.1: The second consultee must not be a doctor.
whyNot.3: The AMHP and managers are not the statutory consultees.

A.q: Under which section can most treatment for mental disorder be given to a detained patient without consent?
options: Section 63
Section 57
Section 117
Section 132
A.why: Section 63: treatment for mental disorder not covered by s57, s58 or s58A may be given without consent by or under the direction of the AC in charge.

whyNot.1: Section 57 covers psychosurgery and needs consent and a second opinion.
whyNot.3: Section 132 is the duty to give information to detained patients.

B.q: Mrs Khan, 54, is detained under section 3, has capacity and refuses ECT. Her condition is not life-threatening. What is the legal position?
options: ECT may be given with a SOAD certificate
ECT may be given under section 63
ECT may be given in her best interests under the MCA
ECT cannot be given while she capably refuses
B.why: Section 58A: a capable adult who refuses cannot be given ECT; the only exception is s62 where it is immediately necessary to save life or prevent serious deterioration.

whyNot.0: A SOAD can certify ECT for a patient who lacks capacity, not override a capable refusal.
whyNot.1: ECT is governed by s58A, not s63.
whyNot.2: MCA s28 bars using the MCA for treatment regulated by Part 4, and she has capacity.

B.q: Leo, 17, detained under section 2, has capacity and consents to ECT. What does the law require?
options: His consent certified by the AC in charge
His parents' written consent
A SOAD certificate as well as his consent
Approval from the Court of Protection
B.why: Section 58A(4): a consenting patient under 18 still needs a SOAD (not the AC in charge) to certify capacity and consent and that ECT is appropriate.

whyNot.0: Certification by the AC in charge is enough for a consenting adult, not someone under 18.
whyNot.1: Parental consent does not replace the s58A safeguard.
whyNot.3: The Court of Protection is not required for s58A ECT.

B.q: Which ground of section 62 urgent treatment can authorise ECT?
options: Immediately necessary to alleviate serious suffering
Immediately necessary to prevent violence
Immediately necessary to save the patient's life
Needed because a SOAD visit is delayed
B.why: Section 62(1A): for ECT, only the grounds of saving life or preventing serious deterioration (not irreversible) apply.

whyNot.0: The serious suffering ground applies to s57 and s58, not ECT.
whyNot.1: The violence ground applies to s57 and s58, not ECT.
whyNot.3: A delayed SOAD visit is not itself a s62 ground.

C.q: Daniel has been on section 3 for 14 weeks, on medication since day 1. A certificate of his capable consent was completed in week 13. Tonight he capably refuses his dose. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Give it, as the week 13 consent certificate is still valid
Withhold it and inform the AC that a SOAD is needed
Give it under section 63 as he is detained
Give it in his best interests under the MCA
C.why: A consent certificate only covers a capable patient who consents. Once Daniel refuses after the three months, s58(3)(b) requires a SOAD certificate, so the nurse should not give it and should inform the AC.

whyNot.0: The certificate relies on his consent, which he has withdrawn.
whyNot.2: After three months, medication is governed by s58, not s63.
whyNot.3: MCA s28 bars the MCA for Part 4 treatment, and he has capacity.

C.q: Mr Bell, detained under section 3, cut his forearm in response to command hallucinations. He has capacity and refuses a dressing. Under the Code of Practice, what can authorise treating the wound?
options: Section 58 with a SOAD certificate
The MCA, in his best interests
Section 63, as ancillary treatment
His consent, as it is physical care
C.why: COP15 24.5: treatment for mental disorder includes physical treatment that is part of, or ancillary to, it, giving the example of treating wounds self-inflicted as a result of mental disorder. Section 63 can therefore apply.

whyNot.0: Section 58 governs medication after three months, not wound care.
whyNot.1: He has capacity, so the MCA cannot authorise treatment he refuses.
whyNot.3: The Code treats self-harm wounds caused by the disorder as within the Act's treatment powers.

C.q: Mrs Grant lacks capacity and is detained under section 3. The SOAD considers ECT appropriate, but she made a valid and applicable advance decision refusing ECT. What follows?
options: The SOAD may certify as she is detained
Her RC may override it as treatment under section 63
Her nearest relative may set it aside
The SOAD cannot certify ECT that conflicts with it
C.why: Section 58A(5)(c): a SOAD certificate for an incapable patient requires that ECT would not conflict with a valid and applicable advance decision (or a decision of an attorney, deputy or the Court of Protection).

whyNot.0: Detention does not override a valid, applicable advance decision about ECT.
whyNot.1: ECT is governed by s58A, not s63.
whyNot.2: The nearest relative has no power over advance decisions.

reteach.title: The ladder of safeguards
reteach.question: Why do some treatments need a certificate and others do not?

blocks.body: Bottom rung: s63, ordinary treatment given under the AC's direction. Next: s58, medication beyond three months needs certified consent or a SOAD. Higher: s58A, ECT, where a capable adult's refusal is respected and under-18s always need a SOAD. Top: s57, psychosurgery, needing consent AND a second opinion for any patient.

blocks.text: Three months runs from the first medication in this detention period, not from admission and not from renewal.

explain.body: Detained patients can be given treatment for mental disorder without consent by or under the direction of the AC in charge, except treatments covered by s57, s58 and s58A.

test.q: Who directs treatment given under section 63?
options: The approved clinician in charge
The second opinion appointed doctor
The hospital managers
The nurse in charge of the shift
test.why: Section 63: treatment is given by or under the direction of the approved clinician in charge of it.

whyNot.1: SOADs certify under s57, s58 and s58A; they do not direct s63 treatment.
whyNot.2: Managers do not direct clinical treatment.
whyNot.3: Nurses give treatment under the AC's direction.

explain.body: After three months from the first medication in this detention, medication needs either the capable patient's consent certified (by the AC or a SOAD) or a SOAD certificate that it is appropriate.

test.q: Who can certify that a capable patient consents to medication under section 58(3)(a)?
options: The AC in charge or a SOAD
The named nurse or ward manager
The AMHP or nearest relative
The GP or community nurse
test.why: Section 58(3)(a): either the AC in charge of the treatment or a SOAD may certify capable consent.

whyNot.3: Neither has a certifying role for in-patient treatment.

explain.body: Capable consenting adult: consent certified. Capable refusal: no ECT unless s62 life-saving or preventing serious deterioration. Incapable: SOAD certificate with no conflict with an advance decision, attorney, deputy or court. Under 18: SOAD always.

test.q: Which decision can prevent a SOAD certifying ECT for a patient who lacks capacity?
options: A nearest relative's objection in writing to managers
A valid and applicable advance decision
The RC's preference for medication
An AMHP's written disagreement
test.why: Section 58A(5)(c): ECT must not conflict with a valid and applicable advance decision or a decision of an attorney, deputy or the Court of Protection.

whyNot.0: The nearest relative cannot veto ECT.
whyNot.2: The RC's preference is not a statutory bar.
whyNot.3: AMHPs have no role in ECT certification.

explain.body: Urgent treatment can be given without the s57 or s58 safeguards if immediately necessary to save life, prevent serious deterioration, alleviate serious suffering, or prevent violence as the minimum interference. ECT: only the first two.

test.q: What must be true of all section 62 urgent treatment?
options: It must be agreed by the nearest relative
It must be given within 72 hours of detention
It must be immediately necessary
It must be approved by a SOAD
test.why: Every s62 ground requires that the treatment is immediately necessary for that purpose.

whyNot.0: The nearest relative has no role in s62.
whyNot.1: There is no 72-hour limit in s62.
whyNot.3: Section 62 applies when the SOAD safeguard cannot be met in time.
